extracted.intended_audience: secondary-school teachers delivering BC First Peoples 12 / educators planning a unit on First Peoples stories and storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and delivering a secondary‑school unit (BC First Peoples 12) on Story and Storytelling that teaches about Oral Traditions, colonization stories, legal uses of oral history, and protocols for working with Indigenous narratives. Includes suggested investigations, assessment strategies, resources, and classroom activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Understanding: Story as method of learning and teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is one of the main methods of traditional First Peoples’ learning and teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that story is central to First Peoples’ cultures and identities and can be placed at the centre of students' learning; used as a container that holds concepts and knowledge in narrative form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Understanding: Forms of First Peoples’ stories
rubrics_metrics.description: First Peoples’ stories take many forms such as prose, song, dance, poetry, theatre, carvings and pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes multimodal nature of stories—recognize and include diverse formats in teaching and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Understanding: Traditional Stories as evidence of connection to territory
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Stories provide evidence that connects First Nations with their Traditional Territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights legal and cultural significance of traditional stories; useful when studying Indigenous rights, land claims and oral history evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Questions for the unit
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the relationships between the Oral Tradition, oral history, and the land? In what ways are cultural values embedded in story? How can you experience a storytelling relationship? What are different ways of telling a story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these guiding questions to shape inquiries, activities and assessments across investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Peoples Principles of Learning (focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning is embedded in memory, history, and story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put story at the centre of students' learning; treat narrative as a vehicle for concepts and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: BC First Peoples 12 Content Standard: Role of oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Role of oral tradition for B.C. First Peoples
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and assess students' understanding of oral tradition's functions in BC First Peoples cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: BC First Peoples 12 Content Standard: Historical exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact of historical exchanges of ideas, practices, and materials among local B.C. First Peoples and with non‑indigenous peoples
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include study of contact, exchange, and influence in classroom investigations and student responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: BC First Peoples 12 Content Standard: Media and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Role and significance of media in challenging and supporting the continuity of culture, language, and self‑determination of B.C. First Peoples
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess student analysis of media's effects on culture, language, and self‑determination (positive and negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: BC First Peoples 12 Content Standard: Contemporary challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary challenges facing B.C. First Peoples, including legacies of colonialism
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect students to identify and analyze contemporary issues and colonial legacies when studying stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: English First Peoples 12 Standard: Oral traditions and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral Traditions: the relationship between oral tradition and land/place
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students' ability to link stories to land/place and protocols for situating oneself in relation to others and place.

rubrics_metrics.name: English First Peoples 12 Standard: Protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Protocols: situating oneself in relation to others and place
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include learning tasks that require students to demonstrate understanding of protocols and relational positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoken Language 12 Standard: Ownership and protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues related to the ownership of First Peoples oral texts and protocols for their use
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address ethical, legal and cultural ownership issues when using or presenting oral texts; evaluate students' awareness of these issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoken Language 12 Standard: Legal status of oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal status of First Peoples oral tradition in Canada
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach cases and legal principles (e.g., Delgamuukw, Tsilhqot’in) and assess students' understanding of oral tradition as legally admissible evidence and its limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary Indigenous Studies 12 Standard: Interconnection of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Varied identities and worldviews of Indigenous peoples, and the importance of the interconnection of family, relationships, language, culture, and the land
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect students to analyze and reflect on interconnectedness in personal and community narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative Assessment Strategy: 3-2-1
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 3-2-1 strategy. Students quickly write down: 3 words that come to mind about Oral Traditions; 2 questions they have; 1 metaphor or simile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a quick assessment of prior knowledge and as a record students can return to later; suitable for whole class or group sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features to note in examples of Oral Traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that highlight Oral Traditions: the song is newly composed based on an ancient origin story; there are Protocols around the use of the song; the rights to use the song have been passed on to the next generation to sing; the Oral Tradition encompasses many dimensions: story, song, dance, ceremony; reference to time frame phrasing (e.g., 'a long time ago – before this time in which we measure').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when viewing/listening to oral tradition examples to guide observation and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom activity outputs (acceptable modes of student response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invite students to respond in ways that make sense to them; examples: written response, Found Poem, questions, visual format, word web/mind map, verbal explanation to a partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow multimodal, culturally relevant responses; use suggested modes as acceptable evidence of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Traditional Stories and narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Many First Peoples classify two main types: (1) ancestral/ancient stories (origins, creation) and (2) more recent event/historical stories. Within these: creation/origin stories; family/House Group/Clan histories; teaching or moral stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students' ability to categorize authentic stories and justify categorization; discuss overlap and multiple meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for writing down Traditional Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss pros and cons of writing down oral stories. Pros: ensures stories live on, preserves language, easier to study. Cons: important aspects lost (physical actions, audience interaction), may contravene Protocols, holders lose control of IP, story may be out of context or incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these points as criteria when evaluating whether/how to transcribe or publish oral stories. Ask: 'Does it matter who writes it down?' and 'What is the best way to record and preserve Traditional Stories?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing numerical data to reveal colonization stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Students analyze population statistics and other tables (e.g., Indigenous Population in Canada Over Time; Stó:lo Population Survey, 1867; Department of Indian Affairs 1920 possessions) to find 'stories' in the numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect activities such as: creating graphs/charts, generating interpretive questions, producing headlines or précis of possible stories, comparing agencies/regions, and suggesting historical explanations for statistical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of colonization stories in contemporary media
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze contemporary formats telling colonization stories: written (fiction, non‑fiction, poetry), spoken word, music, film, animation, graphic novels, personal stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students' ability to identify format, message, and perspective; compile bibliographies and examples; encourage multimodal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delgamuukw principle: oral histories as admissible evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that Delgamuukw (1997) was the first time Canadian courts admitted Traditional Stories and other aspects of Oral Traditions as evidence at trial, entrenching the validity of oral histories as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach the judgment and have students paraphrase the Chief Justice's statements; use as a legal/historical standard when discussing oral evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal considerations: features making oral histories potentially inadmissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that might make oral histories inadmissible before Delgamuukw: they are outside the usual understanding of the court's aim to find facts; they are out‑of‑court statements which could be considered hearsay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as discussion points for why courts must adapt laws of evidence and consider Indigenous ways of knowing; examine the Chief Justice's reasons for accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: case‑by‑case approach to oral traditions in court
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of admitting oral histories 'must be undertaken on a case‑by‑case basis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach nuance—there is no blanket rule; students should evaluate legal contexts individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural accommodation for 'oral traditional evidence' in hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: At NEB hearings (e.g., Trans Mountain) specific time was set aside for 'oral traditional evidence' and Hearing Order/Procedural Direction No. 1 guided the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an example of institutional procedural accommodation; examine transcripts and testimonies to study how procedural directions are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court testimony and Protocols for Elders and Knowledge Keepers
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider issues around Elders delivering Oral Traditions in adversarial settings: cross‑examination may humiliate or interrupt them; they may be reluctant to share knowledge in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask students to identify respectful accommodations and to consult sources (e.g., Discussion Paper on Oral History Evidence in the Federal Court) for suggested practices to protect witnesses and respect Protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating biographies: acceptable formats and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Students can create biographical sketches, visual essays, 'body representation' collages, or podcasts (including imaginary interviews) when creating biographies of Indigenous people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess multimodal projects, encourage journals and literature circles, and require culturally appropriate sourcing and permissions when using living people's stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective learning: 'Give Back, Carry Forward' assessment prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions for reflection: What is one new thing you learned that you would consider a gift? What is one thing growing out of your learning that you can take action on? What did you learn about where you live? What did you learn about yourself?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as prompts for summative reflection, Major Project components, or community action planning; emphasize giving back and carrying forward learning ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protocols for using technology (GPR) in investigations of unmarked burials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of GPR should be respectful and guided by concepts like 'Walking on Two Legs'—incorporate Indigenous knowledge and Western technology; community members should guide site choice, design, process and interpretation; GPR produces 'targets of interest' requiring excavation, time, money, and Protocol; work must be done with respect and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When undertaking sensitive technical work, require community leadership, adherence to protocols, community involvement in interpretation, and plan for respectful follow‑up (excavation, commemoration) consistent with local wishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and Reconciliation Commission Calls to Action (Missing Children and Burial Information 71–76)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls to Action 71–76: make records available to the NCTR; allocate resources to develop/maintain the National Residential School Student Death Register; establish/maintain an online registry of residential school cemeteries; inform families of burial locations and respond to wishes for commemoration/reburial; develop strategies/procedures for identification, documentation, maintenance, commemoration and protection of cemeteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles to follow include: (i) the Aboriginal community most affected shall lead strategy development; (ii) seek information from Survivors and Knowledge Keepers; (iii) respect Aboriginal protocols before potentially invasive technical inspections. Use these as policy/ethical requirements when studying or acting on unmarked burials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protocols of Witnessing (definitions and responsibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnessing: the Aboriginal principle where witnesses are called to be keepers of history for events of historic significance; witnesses store and care for the history they witness and share it with their people; witnessing is a Cultural Protocol and has responsibilities tied to accuracy and recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach the cultural meaning of witnessing, the role of Honorary Witnesses in public inquiries (e.g., TRC), and the expectation that testimony serves both legal/public record and Indigenous practices of witnessing.
